query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Mg-containing lightweight high‐entropy alloys, prolonged thermal exposure activates diffusion-mediated nucleation and growth of fine Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates from the initial metastable solid solution. When these precipitates remain finely and uniformly distributed (particularly along grain interiors), they promote the formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby retaining corrosion and oxidation resistance. However, if the precipitates coarsen or preferentially segregate at grain boundaries, they disrupt the oxide scale continuity and accelerate localized degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal treatment (annealing) at service-relevant temperatures (850–1050°C) for varying durations to induce phase separation.
generation.conditions: A controlled comparison between as-cast (metastable) samples and thermally annealed samples subsequently subjected to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion tests in an oxidizing environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and distribution of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, particularly at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: A diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth process drives the decomposition of the metastable solid solution, forming Mg-rich intermetallic phases. This transformation alters the local chemistry and microstructural interfaces, which in turn modulate the adhesion and continuity of the protective oxide layers formed during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermally treated samples will develop a two-phase microstructure featuring uniformly dispersed fine intermetallic precipitates. When precipitate size and distribution are optimal, the protective oxide scale (e.g., alumina- or chromia-based) will be continuous and more resistant to corrosive attack. In contrast, coarse or grain-boundary concentrated intermetallics will correlate with disrupted oxide layers and faster corrosion/oxidation degradation compared to the pristine metastable state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, homogeneous metastable solid solution exhibits a uniform but relatively lower intrinsic oxide protection due to the absence of stabilized intermetallic phases that could otherwise promote protective oxide formation.
generation.boundary: Service-regime conditions are approximated by prolonged high-temperature exposure (850–1050°C) in oxidizing environments where diffusion is activated, and the kinetics of intermetallic precipitation become significant.
generation.uncertainty: The critical thresholds for precipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution that either enhance or degrade the oxide scale are not precisely known. Moreover, it remains uncertain whether the Mg-rich intermetallics will consistently improve oxide adhesion or might, under certain conditions, lead to localized dealloying and accelerated corrosion.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples: one set remains in the as-cast metastable state and the other undergoes a controlled annealing treatment at 900°C (within the 850–1050°C range) for fixed durations. Subject both sets to accelerated high-temperature oxidation and corrosion tests under identical oxidizing conditions. Employ detailed microstructural and surface analysis (via SEM, TEM, and XRD) to assess intermetallic precipitate formation, oxide scale continuity, and corrosion performance.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of intermetallic phase size, distribution, and volume fraction (using TEM/SEM image analysis)
Phase identification and oxide scale continuity (via XRD and high-resolution microscopy)
Oxidation kinetics (measured as weight gain over time)
Corrosion rates from electrochemical tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant change in intermetallic precipitate characteristics (size/distribution) when compared to the as-cast samples, or if no corresponding differences in oxide scale continuity and corrosion/oxidation performance are observed between the two sets, then the proposed mechanism—that diffusion-driven Mg-rich intermetallic formation mediates the stability of the protective oxide—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization
